title: Recommendation Systems and Customer Goals
objectives: Define candidate generation, scoring, and ranking.
Evaluate top-k recommendations on an appropriate history and denominator.
Compare relevance, novelty, customer goals, and explanation accuracy.

slides.title: A Returning-Customer Decision
bullets: An mHealth user returns to log a meal.
The system chooses among eligible categories using earlier histories.
The objective may include familiar relevance and a stated variety goal.
slides.notes: The next logged basket differs from the next item row. A basket can contain several relevant categories. Availability and the customer's goal constrain which recommendations are useful.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.15, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: The Candidate Set
bullets: Candidate generation determines what can be recommended.
Scoring compares eligible items using current information.
Ranking chooses order and applies list constraints.
slides.notes: A strong ranking model cannot recover an item excluded during candidate generation. Evaluation must retain the candidate-set definition as well as the ranked output.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Recommendation Models
bullets: Content models compare item attributes and customer histories.
Collaborative models learn patterns across customers and items.
Popularity and personal-frequency rules provide useful baselines.
slides.notes: A content model can help with new items that lack interactions. A collaborative model benefits from shared behavior but faces cold-start and selected-exposure problems.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Histories Must Precede the Basket
slides.caption: mHealth evaluation freezes histories and candidate sets at the forecast origin.
slides.description: Training histories precede validation and test baskets. Later outcomes do not define candidate eligibility or tune the final model.
slides.notes: Returning-user prediction can use the user's earlier history while holding out later baskets. The distinction is temporal rather than necessarily a complete user holdout.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.15.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Recall Among Relevant Categories
slides.intro: Let $L_i$ be the top-k list and $B_i$ the categories in the next observed basket.
slides.interpretation: The denominator is the number of relevant basket categories for that user-event.
slides.notes: Report how empty baskets and unavailable categories are handled. Average per event or per user according to the target population, and retain the chosen weighting rule.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Position Matters
slides.intro: Discount lower-ranked relevant items when their positions affect exposure.
slides.interpretation: NDCG divides by the best attainable DCG for the same relevance labels.
slides.notes: NDCG depends on the candidate set and relevance definition. Unobserved engagement is not necessarily a negative preference label because exposure is selective.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Basket Associations
bullets: Support counts how often items occur together.
Confidence conditions on the antecedent item.
Lift compares confidence with the consequent's marginal prevalence.
slides.notes: Association rules are descriptive. A positive lift can reflect common meal occasions or other causes rather than a response to recommendation. Evaluate rules on later baskets.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.17, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Lift Changes the Baseline Comparison
slides.caption: mHealth basket rules use distinct baskets and future validation.
slides.description: The chart compares rule confidence with a marginal-prevalence benchmark. Common items can have high confidence with little lift.
slides.notes: Counting item rows instead of distinct baskets changes the denominator and can inflate associations through repeated entries.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.17, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Relevance and a Customer Goal
slides.intro: Combine relevance $s_j$ with a goal score $g_j$ using an explicit weight.
slides.interpretation: The scores need a comparable scale before the weight has a clear interpretation.
slides.notes: A goal score should reflect a defined customer objective and validated measurement. The weight does not become a preference estimate merely because a programmer sets it.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.12.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Small Weight Changes Can Change the First Item
slides.caption: Synthetic item scores. Relevance and goal scores stay fixed.
slides.description: A ranks first at low goal weights, B in a middle range, and C at high weights. The maximizing item switches at crossings even though each score changes smoothly.
slides.notes: A recommendation can be discontinuous in a tuning weight. Sensitivity analysis should report the ranking itself, not only smooth average scores.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.12.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: A Three-Item Basket Check
slides.intro: The list contains A, B, and C. The basket contains A and C.
slides.code:
from math import log2
ranked = ['A', 'B', 'C']
relevant = {'A', 'C'}
recall = len(set(ranked) & relevant) / len(relevant)
dcg = sum((x in relevant) / log2(r+2)
          for r,x in enumerate(ranked))
ideal = 1 + 1/log2(3)
assert recall == 1.0
slides.check: Recall is 1.0, while NDCG is about 0.920 because B occupies the second position.
slides.notes: The calculation uses binary relevance. It assumes all relevant items are eligible and that the observation window defines a valid basket.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: LLM Explanations
bullets: Explain a recommendation using verified item attributes.
Check whether stated reasons are factually supported.
Evaluate explanation effects separately from ranking quality.
slides.notes: An explanation can sound plausible while inventing a nutritional property or claiming a nonexistent personal preference. Factual support and behavioral effects require distinct evaluations.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.13, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Offline and Online Outcomes
bullets: A hit in a historical basket measures predictive overlap.
A recommendation changes exposure and may change behavior.
A randomized policy comparison measures the intervention outcome.
slides.notes: A historically unrecorded category can be unknown rather than disliked. Offline metrics are informative under their measurement conditions but do not identify the effect of displaying a new list.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.15, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Personalization Can Improve Consumer Welfare
bullets: A ranking experiment found more search and purchasing.
Its structural model estimated higher consumer surplus despite profit weighting.
Separate experimental behavior from model-dependent welfare.
slides.notes: Welfare Effects of Personalized Rankings compares personalized rankings with uniform bestseller rankings. The claim here follows the verified publisher abstract; the final full text was not retrieved. Targeted Advertising as Implicit Recommendation supplies a theoretical counterpoint in which strategic targeting and endogenous prices alter welfare. Neither study establishes that all personalization helps or harms consumers. See M7 Section 7.21.
slides.source: https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.1441 and https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0117

slides.title: Coding Exercise: Ranking With a Goal
bullets: Compare popularity and personal-frequency baselines.
Tune the goal weight on validation baskets.
Evaluate the fixed choice on later baskets.
Assess one generated explanation against item attributes.
slides.notes: Run ../03_Data_and_Code/Lecture_Examples/session_examples.py S12 for the NDCG check. The full mHealth m07.py program defines the candidate and basket windows. Preserve the final test period for evaluation.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Customer Control of Recommendations
bullets: A customer can accept a suggested goal or reject it.
Factual explanations should distinguish evidence from an inferred preference.
Evaluate whether the interface respects a revised goal.
slides.notes: A nominal control that does not affect the recommendation can leave the customer unable to change the policy. A recommendation evaluation should record both the chosen setting and its implemented effect.
slides.source: ETHICS_AND_REGULATION.md, M7.

slides.title: Recommendation Discussion
bullets: Which relevant item was excluded before scoring?
Whose goal determines the ranking weight?
What evidence would show improved customer experience?
slides.notes: The full policy includes eligibility, ranking, explanation, and updates after use. A useful evaluation identifies which component changed.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.12, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

practice: Compare ranking baselines, calculate NDCG, and assess a goal-weight sensitivity.
application: Check a generated recommendation explanation and design an online outcome comparison.

title: Adaptive Recommendations and Marketing Budgets
objectives: Trace how recommendations affect future training data.
Evaluate list objectives and customer goals.
Allocate a fixed marketing budget using marginal response.

slides.title: Recommendations Shape the Paths Customers Follow
slides.description: A gardener consults a tablet beside familiar and exploratory paths through different fruit trees. The paths represent selected exposure and future opportunities.
slides.notes: A frequently used path produces more observations from its existing destinations. Exploration changes which preferences can be learned.
slides.source: Original conceptual illustration. 05_Slides/assets/PROVENANCE.md.

slides.title: An Adaptive Policy
bullets: A model selects exposure using existing interaction histories.
Customers respond to the displayed options.
Retraining incorporates those selected responses.
slides.notes: The policy changes the environment that supplies future training data. The update rule and retraining schedule belong in the definition of the intervention.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Selected Exposure Creates a Feedback Loop
slides.caption: The diagram describes a policy mechanism rather than an estimated effect.
slides.description: Recommendations affect exposure, exposure affects observed responses, and those responses inform subsequent training and recommendations.
slides.notes: A popularity loop can concentrate observation among already visible items. Randomized exploration or additional evaluation data can change what the system learns.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: The Evaluation Horizon Includes Learning
slides.caption: A temporary intervention can persist through subsequent model updates.
slides.description: The intervention changes responses during the campaign. A retrained model can preserve information from those responses after the campaign ends.
slides.notes: Freezing the model blocks the retraining channel but can leave direct changes in customer behavior. These policies require separate definitions and, where feasible, separate comparisons.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.1.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Customer Goals and Platform Objectives
bullets: Clicks reveal a response within an offered environment.
Considered preferences can differ from immediate engagement.
Measure satisfaction, unwanted repetition, and customer-stated goals.
slides.notes: A higher click count can coexist with regret or frustration. A system can combine behavior with explicit goals while recognizing that each measure has its own errors.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.2.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: A List Objective
slides.intro: A list combines item relevance with category variety.
slides.interpretation: The variety weight $\lambda$ is expressed in the same units as the relevance score.
slides.notes: A weighted sum requires a substantive choice of scales and tradeoffs. A customer replenishing a familiar basket may prefer a different weight from a customer seeking variety.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Two Three-Item Lists
slides.caption: Synthetic scores. The lists tie at a variety weight of 0.20.
slides.notes: A and B are coffee, C is tea, and D is fruit. The variety gain trades off against 0.20 of relevance. The values are imposed teaching scores.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Model-Based and Experimental Evidence
bullets: A fitted choice model can compare alternative recommenders.
A randomized perturbation can test predicted response patterns.
Engagement, retention, revenue, and welfare are distinct outcomes.
slides.notes: The Netflix study discussed in the notes uses a fitted choice model and an experimental check. Its replacement-recommender comparisons are model-based counterfactuals with specific exposure conditions.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.1.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Marketing-Mix Modeling
bullets: Weekly channel spending can have delayed effects.
Response can saturate at high exposure.
Spending decisions can respond to anticipated demand.
slides.notes: Trend, seasonality, promotions, and media can move together. A fitted media component requires an identification argument before it is interpreted as a causal contribution.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.3, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Carryover
slides.intro: A geometric accumulated-exposure measure retains earlier spending.
slides.interpretation: A 100-unit pulse with $\rho=0.5$ gives 100, 50, 25, and 12.5 in successive periods.
slides.notes: This definition is unnormalized. Under constant spending s, its long-run level is s divided by one minus rho. Coefficients must follow the implementation's normalization.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.3, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Saturation and the Next Dollar
slides.intro: A concave response has declining marginal contribution.
slides.interpretation: Budget transfers depend on marginal response at the current allocation.
slides.notes: Average response summarizes all earlier units of spending. The next small transfer depends on the local slope, with units of contribution per spending unit.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Average and Marginal Returns Can Disagree
slides.caption: Synthetic known response curves. Total spending is fixed at 60 thousand dollars.
slides.description: At the starting allocation, A has higher average return while B has higher marginal return. A transfer from A to B increases total contribution.
slides.notes: The response curves are 100 times one minus exp(-sA/20) and 80 times one minus exp(-sB/40). The interior allocation equalizes marginal returns.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: The Fixed-Budget Optimum
slides.intro: Solve equal marginal returns for the imposed curves.
slides.code:
from math import exp, log
budget = 60
a = (log(2.5) + budget/40) / (1/20 + 1/40)
b = budget - a
ma = 5 * exp(-a/20)
mb = 2 * exp(-b/40)
assert abs(ma-mb) < 1e-12
slides.check: The allocation is about 32.22 to A and 27.78 to B, in thousands of dollars.
slides.notes: The closed-form result applies to these known concave curves and an interior fixed-budget optimum. Different constraints or uncertain response functions require a revised calculation.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Coding Exercise: A Policy Objective
bullets: Enumerate three-item lists at several variety weights.
Solve and independently grid-check the fixed-budget allocation.
Report the assumptions that change the preferred action.
slides.notes: Run ../03_Data_and_Code/Lecture_Examples/session_examples.py S13. A grid check verifies the numerical optimum within its resolution. It does not establish the imposed response curves as causal estimates.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Attention and the Optimization Target
bullets: A free service can require customer time and attention.
More exposure can benefit advertisers while burdening customers.
Evaluate voluntary use and customer outcomes alongside engagement.
slides.notes: Tim Wu's Blind Spot discusses attention markets and the difficulty of analyzing exchanges without a monetary user price. A course application should measure time, control, and value rather than equate engagement with welfare.
slides.source: Tim Wu, Blind Spot: The Attention Economy and the Law (2019). https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/2029/

slides.title: Policy Discussion
bullets: What changes when the recommender learns during the experiment?
Which outcome measures the customer's stated goal?
How much uncertainty in response slopes would change the budget?
slides.notes: A robust decision states the learning rule, target outcome, and support for the response function. The best numerical optimizer cannot supply those definitions.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.7, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

practice: Compare list objectives and solve a budget allocation with an independent grid check.
application: Design a comparison that separates temporary exposure from subsequent learning.

title: Generative AI, Consumer Choice, and Regulation
objectives: Assess AI demand measurements and workflow claims.
Explain why a commercial objective can conflict with customer interests.
Map a marketing decision to the relevant evidence, jurisdiction, and rule status.
Examine the premises connecting commercial results to customer-benefit claims.
Compare Kantian, institutional, and Confucian reasons for a marketing recommendation.

slides.title: A Subscription-Growth Decision
bullets: A firm wants to increase paid renewals.
The evidence includes subscription histories, interfaces, and customer outcomes.
A higher renewal rate can arise through improved value or greater cancellation friction.
slides.notes: The commercial outcome does not identify the consumer mechanism. A useful assessment records value, consent, cancellation completion, and customer time as well as revenue.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.13, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Public Attention and Paid Demand
bullets: Pageviews measure attention to selected pages.
Paid subscriptions measure a specific payment relationship.
User, provider, and category denominators differ.
slides.notes: A title change can split attention across pages. A user can hold multiple subscriptions. These measurement choices can create apparent differences in demand without the same underlying object.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.13, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: A Fixed Starting Cohort
slides.caption: Entirely synthetic subscription panel. Provider labels identify simulated options.
slides.description: Starting-provider cohorts split into same-provider, other-provider-only, and no-paid-provider states. Each bar uses its own fixed starting cohort denominator.
slides.notes: These simulated percentages are not actual market shares or provider retention estimates. Multiple-provider behavior requires a definition that prevents incompatible categories from being added.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Subscriber Stocks and New Flows
bullets: A subscriber stock includes past acquisition and survival.
A new-subscription flow can include first purchases and returns.
A price coefficient depends on the outcome and behavioral model.
slides.notes: Regressing subscriber stocks on current prices can combine persistent state with current choice. A structural interpretation must match the data-generating choice process.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.13.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: A Known Model Is a Useful Verification Case
slides.caption: Synthetic demand exercise with a known binary-model benchmark.
slides.description: The exact binary benchmark recovers a price coefficient of -0.06. Stock and new-flow specifications give different coefficients under their different data definitions.
slides.notes: Recovering the benchmark checks implementation under its assumptions. It does not establish a structural interpretation for the richer simulated panel or actual market data.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.13.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Seller Costs and Customer Alternatives
slides.caption: Hypothetical dollars per customer, conditional on 50 sales.
slides.description: The initial seller floor is 40 dollars and buyer ceiling 80. Seller automation lowers the floor to 30 while the ceiling stays 80. Shared adoption raises outside-option utility and lowers the ceiling to 20, below the 30-dollar floor.
slides.notes: Delivered value is 200 dollars, buyer burden 40, and fixed cost 1,000. Unit cost falls from 20 to 10. Outside-option utility then rises from 80 to 140. Gray intervals indicate simultaneous weak participation and cost recovery. Volume and valuations are imposed; these bounds neither estimate demand nor solve a pricing equilibrium. Customers are indifferent at the ceiling.
slides.source: Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes, M8 §8.17.2.

slides.title: AI Workflow Quality
bullets: Measure the completed analysis and its validity.
Include generation, review, and repair time.
Use comparable tasks and independent quality criteria.
slides.notes: A time comparison can favor a tool because it abandons difficult tasks or reduces quality. The outcome definition should account for completion and validity before comparing speed.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.6, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Review Time Is Part of Production
slides.caption: Synthetic workflows meet the same stated quality requirement.
slides.description: Manual production and review total 110 minutes. Assisted production and review total 85 minutes, a 22.7% total reduction despite a 50% drafting-time reduction.
slides.notes: The manual workflow uses 90 minutes to produce and 20 to review. The assisted workflow uses 45 and 40. These are imposed time inputs, not an estimate of a universal AI effect.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.6, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Reuse Has a Break-Even Workload
slides.caption: Hypothetical equal-quality work: six setup hours, with adaptation included.
slides.description: The existing process takes two hours per use. The reusable process takes six setup hours plus 1.5 hours per use, including upkeep. The lines cross at twelve uses and total 48 versus 42 hours at twenty-four uses.
slides.notes: Execution alone falls from two hours to 1.25, but 0.25 upkeep hours are required per use. Net savings become positive at the thirteenth use. Twenty-four uses save six hours, a 12.5% reduction after setup and upkeep. The numbers are imposed and do not measure course development time. Run investment.py and vary upkeep or workload.
slides.source: Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes, M8 §8.17.1.

slides.title: Model Updates and Unresolved Tasks
bullets: Identify the changed model, prompt, tool, data, or evaluation rule.
Compare paired cases and fresh tasks using the same criteria.
Include regressions, review costs, and customer consequences in the decision.
slides.notes: A new release motivates a hypothesis about the current workflow. It does not establish improvement in the intended task population. Preserve the current procedure, predefine acceptance criteria, and retain a way to return to it. The claim-lifetime study motivates task-specific revalidation; it does not set a universal review interval.
slides.source: M8 §8.18.1; M7 §7.22. https://zou-group.github.io/llm-claims-shelf-life/

slides.title: Residual Risk and Scale
bullets: An expired research category can still allow residual failures.
Expected failure loss depends on uses, failure probability, and consequences.
Verify that references exist and support the claims made.
slides.notes: A fitted category describes the source protocol and selected model panel. The relevant deployment criterion depends on customer outcomes and exposure. A decline in fabricated references leaves other checks necessary, including correct details and support for an assertion. Correct references do not identify authorship.
slides.source: M8 §8.18.1; M2 §2.21. ../01_Resources/14_LLM_Evidence_and_Revalidation/README.md

slides.title: Marketing Dialectics: Examine the Premise
bullets: State the claim, its evidence, and the premise connecting them.
Kant examines reason’s demand for an unconditioned explanation.
A marketing analogy must preserve the scope of the original argument.
slides.notes: Kant’s transcendental dialectic concerns metaphysical cognition. These marketing cases adapt the practice of examining premises; an ordinary empirical dispute is not a cosmological antinomy. The third antinomy does not imply that accurate purchase prediction proves lost agency. Critical examination may support, restrict, or reject a claim; no forced synthesis is required.
slides.source: Marketing Dialectics, §§9.1–9.3. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md

slides.title: Commercial Results and Customer Claims
slides.caption: Causal, measurement, and ethical questions have different premises.
slides.description: Separate paths connect a practice to commercial effects and customer outcomes. A judgment about the practice also requires an ethical principle.
slides.notes: A randomized intervention can establish incremental purchases without establishing informed choice or customer benefit. Kant’s humanity formulation supplies a distinct ethical question about treatment of persons.
slides.source: Marketing Dialectics, §§9.1, 9.4. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md

slides.title: Self-Interest Creates a Burden of Justification
slides.caption: A reason for scrutiny is distinct from evidence of misconduct.
slides.description: A material conflict leads to independent substantiation and then a decision that can change with evidence.
slides.notes: Hume proposes institutional checks that work under private-interest pursuit and distinguishes that design maxim from universal dishonesty. Smith urges scrutiny of interested commercial-regulation proposals. Requiring firms to substantiate customer-benefit claims is a contemporary institutional recommendation, not a universal legal presumption of guilt.
slides.source: Marketing Dialectics, §9.10. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md

slides.title: Confucian Perspectives: Profit and Responsibility
bullets: Evaluate how profit is obtained and which relationships sustain it.
A trusted adviser or customer-care role carries standards of conduct.
Examine whether the claimed role matches incentives and practice.
slides.notes: Analects 4.5 and 4.16 place righteousness in the evaluation of gain; Mencius 1A.1 challenges an exclusive focus on advantage. Analects 12.7 and 13.3 motivate trustworthiness and fit between names, roles, and conduct. These are contemporary applications of texts with historical political settings. A profitable exchange can serve both parties.
slides.source: Marketing Dialectics, §§9.11.1–9.11.2. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md

slides.title: Truthful Challenge and Cultivated Judgment
bullets: Harmony can include reasoned disagreement.
Learning and reflection should discipline an AI-generated answer.
Good conduct depends on repeated practices as well as stated values.
slides.notes: Analects 13.23, 14.22, and 2.15 support discussion of truthful challenge and reflective learning. Mencius emphasizes cultivable moral beginnings; Xunzi emphasizes deliberate effort, teaching, and ritual. They disagree about human nature. A modern firm can examine what its rewards teach employees to notice and whether an analyst can report an unwanted customer outcome.
slides.source: Marketing Dialectics, §§9.11.3–9.11.4. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md

slides.title: A Choice Procedure Can Change Renewal
bullets: A direct offer and an offer preceded by questions can produce different choices.
The customer still makes the final selection.
An independent value measure determines whether an additional renewal benefits that customer.
slides.notes: Questions, defaults, or retention prompts can precede a fixed target decision. The welfare comparison depends on consumer values, stable response probabilities, and the procedure set. A renewal increase alone does not establish either benefit or harm.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Opposed Interests
slides.intro: Suppose renewal yields firm margin $\nu>0$ and costs the customer $\sigma>0$ relative to declining.
slides.interpretation: A higher renewal probability raises profit and lowers customer value under these stated stakes.
slides.notes: This conditional comparison holds the offer, monetary values, and relevant response population fixed. It does not infer customer harm from conversion alone. Additional time and authority costs require separate measurement.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Profit and Customer Value Can Move Oppositely
slides.caption: Synthetic probabilities and fixed stakes. Direct renewal is 20%.
slides.description: An optional procedure lowers renewal to 10%; another raises it to 60%. At firm margin 11 dollars and customer loss 10 dollars per unwanted renewal, the latter gains the firm 4.40 dollars and costs the customer 4 dollars relative to direct choice.
slides.notes: The direct-choice benchmark is distinct from the consumer-preferred procedure. Relative to the 10% procedure, the 60% procedure creates a 5-dollar customer loss. These probabilities and monetary values are imposed inputs, not observed customer responses.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Experimentation Selects the Commercial Winner
bullets: A fixed set of procedures has stable renewal probabilities.
Independent randomized samples estimate each probability.
With opposed interests, accurately selecting the largest rate also selects the largest loss in that set.
slides.notes: The result requires common fixed stakes, a fixed catalog chosen before the experiment, stable responses from experiment to deployment, and complete independently sampled outcomes. It does not say that every experiment harms consumers.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: A Cancellation Evaluation
bullets: Include a direct-cancellation comparison.
Record whether optional retention content can be refused before exposure.
Measure completion, elapsed time, subsequent charges, and customer value.
slides.notes: An effective refusal path and an independent value measure reveal dimensions hidden by renewals. A direct-choice arm helps isolate the effect of the preceding interaction.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: A Welfare Comparison
slides.intro: Synthetic stakes distinguish profit from customer value.
slides.code:
direct, selected = 0.20, 0.60
firm_margin, customer_loss = 11, 10
firm_gain = firm_margin * (selected-direct)
value_change = -customer_loss * (selected-direct)
assert round(firm_gain, 2) == 4.40
assert round(value_change, 2) == -4.00
slides.check: Higher combined surplus can coexist with a customer loss under these assumptions.
slides.notes: The combined change is 0.40 dollars per potential customer in this example. The welfare result is conditional on the imposed values. A choice probability does not independently reveal those values.

title: Integrated Decisions and Final Presentations
objectives: Connect validated analysis to a concrete marketing decision.
Evaluate uncertainty, consumer consequences, and operational constraints.
Communicate a reproducible conclusion and a useful next test.

slides.title: An Integrated Marketing Decision
bullets: Choose a feasible action and a defined customer population.
Connect measurement, modeling, and evaluation to that action.
State the costs, customer outcomes, and uncertainty that affect the choice.
slides.notes: The evidence chain can include a descriptive assessment, a predictive model, a causal comparison, and a scenario. Each component should retain its own scope and assumptions.

slides.title: The Evidence Behind the Recommendation
bullets: State the sample, observation unit, and outcome horizon.
Show the comparison that supports the main claim.
Explain which result changes the recommended action.
slides.notes: A result becomes decision-relevant when it changes a feasible choice under explicit costs or constraints. The audience should be able to assess the supporting comparison directly.

slides.title: A Calculation the Audience Can Check
bullets: Trace one figure to an aggregate table and source records.
Reproduce one prediction, coefficient interpretation, or policy value.
Retain complete code and data definitions with the result.
slides.notes: A hand-checkable calculation complements complete reproducible code. It provides independent evidence about the unit, denominator, and direction of the computation.

slides.title: A Result That Could Change the Decision
bullets: Identify the most consequential uncertain parameter.
Show the threshold at which the preferred action changes.
Consider a feasible test that could resolve that uncertainty.
slides.notes: Sensitivity should connect uncertainty to action. A wide parameter range is useful when it reveals whether the decision is stable or fragile.

slides.title: Customer Consequences
bullets: Report effects on access, time, value, and unwanted charges where relevant.
Distinguish voluntary continued use from difficulty leaving.
Explain how customers can refuse or correct the proposed interaction.
slides.notes: The relevant customer outcome depends on the product and action. A higher platform metric can conceal costs outside the optimized objective.

slides.title: Regulatory Scope
bullets: Identify the jurisdiction and covered conduct.
Separate the current rule from a proposal or allegation.
Match the evidence supporting a claim to what customers will understand.
slides.notes: The primary-source record should identify the effective date and consequential exclusions. A legal conclusion for one sector or jurisdiction should not be transferred mechanically to another.

slides.title: Presentation Discussion
bullets: Is the recommendation supported for the stated population?
What analytical or customer risk has the largest consequence?
Which part of the result can be reproduced independently?
slides.notes: Feedback should name an observable gap in the evidence or a specific counterexample. The strongest response supplies a corrected comparison or explains why the original remains valid.

slides.title: A Deployment Comparison
bullets: Retain a benchmark and a defined evaluation population.
Monitor outcomes and data coverage after the action changes behavior.
Set a response when quality or customer outcomes deteriorate.
slides.notes: A policy that changes exposure can also change future training data. Evaluation after deployment needs versioned inputs, outcomes, and policy rules.

slides.title: An Evidence-Based Recommendation
bullets: Name the action, expected consequence, and decision threshold.
Keep consequential uncertainty beside the estimate.
Identify the next concrete extension supported by the evidence.
slides.notes: A conditional recommendation can be decisive when its conditions are measurable. The final decision should remain traceable to the data, assumptions, and customer outcomes.

practice: Presentation blocks with evidence, reproducibility, and customer-outcome discussion.
application: Compare recommendations using decision thresholds and identify the next useful test.
